title: AHC Port
description: One seam between the harness and something outside it. A port states WHAT MUST HOLD across the seam, which capabilities it participates in, what stays on the harness side of it, and what an outside implementation supplies. It is declared as data: no signatures, no types, no language. A port never names a product, never states a verification obligation, and is never a partition of the catalog — most capabilities are structural and have no port at all.

port.description: The port name. Permanent and never reused — this is the interchange vocabulary, and renaming one breaks every profile that binds it. Layer and archetype are metadata, never part of the name.

status.description: Deprecated ports stay declared forever so existing bindings keep resolving.

tier.description: 'core' — a harness of any shape has this seam. 'extension' — pulled in by archetype, and requires_archetypes says which. Mirrors the catalog's own core/delta split so a single-turn transform never has to think about approval queues.

requires_archetypes.description: Required for extension ports, forbidden for core ones.

direction.description: 'consumed' — the harness calls out through this seam. 'exported' — the harness offers this seam to something else, which is a genuinely different shape and the reason evaluation gets bolted on late when it is not modelled.

serves.description: Capabilities this seam participates in. Participation is not ownership: a capability listed here is usually shared with the harness side, and the split is stated in kernel_owns.

kernel_owns.description: What stays on the harness side of the seam and is therefore not an implementation's to decide. This field is what stops a port from quietly becoming a client library — if everything is on the far side, the seam is a wrapper.

supplied_outside.description: What an implementation on the far side actually provides. Stated as a class of thing, never as a product.

operations.description: What passes through the seam, by intent. No signatures, no types, no language — those belong to a generated interface, not to the specification.

optional.description: True when an implementation may legitimately not offer it, in which case the harness must have a declared path for its absence.

invariants.description: What must hold across this seam whoever implements it. This is the substance of a port — a seam with no invariants is a naming convention.

key.description: Optional, permanent once given. The name a conformance case uses for the invariant it checks, as `port/key`, the way a profile names a decision as `AHC-####/key`. Renaming one breaks every suite that cited it, so a key is never reused or changed; an invariant that stops being right is reworded under the same key only if every case written against it still means the same thing.

because.description: What breaks when it does not hold. Same discipline as failure_mode on a capability: a vague one means the invariant is a preference.

checkable.description: How an adopter could establish it holds. 'declared' means neither a static rule nor a replayable test can reach it, so it has to be asserted and owned — and that is worth knowing before anyone claims coverage.

standards.description: Optional. Published specifications that already define all or part of this seam's wire — a protocol, an envelope, a set of semantic conventions. Cited, never required: an implementation that conforms to one supplies the operations it covers, and the port's invariants hold on top of it whoever supplies them. A port cites a standard rather than restating it, which is principle 1 applied to the seam. The only place in a port that may carry a proper name, because a citation of a specification is not an endorsement of a product.

kind.description: 'open-standard' — maintained by a standards body or an open governance process. 'de-facto' — one vendor's interface that many others accept. Saying which is the honesty that keeps a citation from reading as a standard it is not.

covers.description: Which of this port's operations the specification defines a wire for. The linter checks each is an operation of this port. An operation no standard covers is the harness's own, and is where a typed signature would be needed if one ever is.

substitution_test.description: What proves this is a port rather than one implementation's API with a wrapper on it: the swap that must be possible, and what may legitimately differ afterwards. If no such swap can be described, the seam is in the wrong place.
